extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and rules for legitimate induction and the relation between deduction and induction in scientific and practical inquiries. Explains what counts as induction, what does not, and how to test the validity of inductive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive sciences are hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of all Deductive Sciences is hypothetical: they proceed by tracing the consequences of certain assumptions, leaving for separate consideration whether the assumptions are true or not, and if not exactly true, whether they are a sufficiently near approximation to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using deduction in sciences other than pure number, explicitly identify the assumptions and then (a) determine by observation or argument how closely they approximate truth for the case at hand, and (b) use pre-worked-out consequences of those assumptions so as to minimize ad-hoc reasoning when specific cases arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty limited to pure Number
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) is not an attribute of all mathematical truths, but only of those which relate to pure Number, and only so long as we abstain from supposing numbers to be precise indices to actual quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute absolute certainty to geometrical or mechanical conclusions unless you also justify the truth of their underlying suppositions; distinguish certainty of inference from certainty of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrative science as analysis of consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative Science consists in inquiring what else may be concluded if we find, and in proportion as we find, the assumptions to be true — an inquiry that may be performed once for all and held ready for use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and catalogue consequences of given assumptions in advance so they can be applied rapidly when those assumptions are accepted; this separates deriving consequences from testing premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction can yield novel truths from assumed facts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is practicable to arrive at new conclusions from facts assumed as well as from facts observed; deduction consists of a series of inferences that can reveal truths inaccessible to direct observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing deduction from assumed premises, be explicit that conclusions depend on those assumptions; use deductive chains (including reductio ad absurdum) to test the consistency and implications of assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of demonstrative evidence and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: That is necessary from which to withhold our assent would be to violate the axiom that whatever has a mark has what it is a mark of; nothing is necessary except the connexion between a conclusion and premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat logical necessity as the necessity of inferential connexion: test whether denying the conclusion while admitting the premises would infringe the fundamental maxim of ratiocination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the operation of discovering and proving general propositions: the process by which we infer that what we know to be true in particular cases will be true in all cases which resemble the former in certain assignable respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming general propositions, specify (a) the observed particulars, (b) the class of resembling cases (assignable respects), and (c) the justification why the observed instances warrant universal application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same principles govern general and individual inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles and rules of inference are the same whether we infer general propositions or individual facts; a complete logic of the sciences would be a complete logic of all legitimate inference from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same inductive tests and legitimacy criteria to single-case inferences as to generalizations; do not treat 'individual fact' proofs as a separate logical species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of appropriate inductions requires sagacity
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical inquiries the chief difficulty lies not in making inductions but in choosing among known general propositions those which furnish marks to trace whether the subject possesses the predicate — a task dependent on natural or acquired sagacity and domain knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'which general rule to apply' is often not codifiable; rely on expertise and domain familiarity to select the most relevant inductions rather than expecting mechanical rules to generate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of an argument is tripartite
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of an argument depends on (1) the senses or testimony for individual facts, (2) the rules of the syllogism to determine whether facts fit induction templates, and (3) the legitimacy of the inductions themselves decided by other rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an argument, separately assess: empirical correctness of data, correctness of logical combination (syllogistic form), and the inductive legitimacy (sampling, relevance, counterinstances, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction excludes mere abbreviation/registration of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: An operation that simply restates facts known of every individual of a class (a shorthand registration) is not an induction, because it involves no inference from known to unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating exhaustive enumeration or compact notation of observed individuals as inductive proof; label such operations as descriptive summarization rather than induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction excludes 'induction by parity of reasoning' (mathematical summation)
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions obtained by summing up a series of particular demonstrative proofs or by diagrammatic demonstration (induction by parity of reasoning) are not proper inductions because they rest on a priori demonstrative evidence rather than inference from particular instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine empirical induction from mathematical generalization derived from demonstration or a priori considerations; do not conflate the two when defending empirical generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish description (summing observed parts) from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere description of a set of observed phenomena — combining piecemeal observations into a general conception (e.g., expressing a coastline as an island after circumnavigation) — is not induction unless it involves an inference beyond the observed data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing a complex phenomenon from partial observations, explicitly ask whether the conclusion asserts anything beyond the observed parts; only if it infers unobserved regularity or future continuation is it induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate induction requires justifying inference to resembling cases
rubrics_metrics.description: We may infer that what is true of certain individuals of a class is true of the whole class only when the cases 'resemble the former in certain assignable respects' and the evidence justifies the generalization to all such resembling cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the 'assignable respects' that define the relevant class and provide argument or observation showing why resemblance in those respects licenses extension of the predicate to the whole class; check for counterexamples and boundary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction applies equally to predicting individual unknowns and to general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the evidence derived from observation of known cases justifies drawing an inference about one unknown case, the same evidence would justify drawing a similar inference about a whole class of cases that resemble the observed ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat single-case predictions and general law-claims as logically different in kind; use the same standards of evidential support and similarity of circumstances for both.
